sections.b: Exodus 12 gives the rite before the event. On the tenth of the first month (Abib, later Nisan) each household chooses a lamb or young goat without defect; on the fourteenth it is slaughtered "between the two evenings," its blood is daubed with hyssop on the doorposts and lintel, and it is eaten roasted, whole, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, by people dressed for travel. "I will see the blood and pass over you" (12:13). The meal is followed by seven days of unleavened bread, and the whole is to be kept "for all time." Children's questions (12:26; 13:8, 14) are built into the rite, and outsiders may join if circumcised (12:48).

The noun pesach comes from the verb pasach, usually "pass over, skip." Isaiah 31:5 uses the verb beside "shield" and "rescue," and the Targums and Mekhilta render "have pity on" or "protect," so some scholars translate "the LORD will stand guard over the door." Many critical scholars think the rite began as a spring protection sacrifice of herders and was later joined to the farmers' Feast of Unleavened Bread; Exodus gives every part of it a meaning tied to the night of the exodus.

sections.h: Passover in Jewish and Christian practice
sections.b: After the Temple fell in AD 70, the home Seder replaced the sacrifice: four cups linked to the verbs of Exodus 6:6–7, the child's questions, the story of the exodus, the bitter herbs and matzah, and the Hallel psalms (Mishnah, Pesachim 10). Samaritans still slaughter lambs on Mount Gerizim. Christians kept Pascha, Easter, as the feast of Christ's death and resurrection at Passover time: "Our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered" (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Gospels set the Last Supper at Passover (whether it was itself a Passover meal is debated: Jeremias for, John P. Meier against), and John notes that none of Jesus' bones was broken (Exodus 12:46).

common: The blood on the doorposts marked the households the LORD would spare on the night of the tenth plague.
uncommon: Some scholars read pesach as "protect" rather than "pass over," so that the LORD stands guard at the door against the destroyer.

claude.title: A rite that outlived its altar
claude.body: Passover may have begun as a protective spring rite, but Exodus remade it into a rite of memory and identity, telling each generation to say "what the LORD did for me." That shift, more than anything else, explains how the festival survived the end of sacrifice in AD 70. This is my own reading.

sections.b: Exodus 7–12 tells of ten blows on Egypt: blood, frogs, gnats, swarms, livestock disease, sores, hail, locusts, darkness, and the death of the firstborn. They fall into three sets of three before the tenth: in each set the first begins with a morning meeting by the river, the second with a warning in the palace, the third with no warning. From the fourth blow, Goshen is spared. The magicians copy the first two, fail at the third ("It is the finger of God," 8:19), and are struck by the sixth. Psalms 78 and 105 list the plagues in different orders and numbers.

Greta Hort (1957) proposed a natural sequence: a red, algae-laden Nile flood, fleeing frogs, insects breeding in their remains, cattle disease and skin anthrax, a winter hailstorm, wind-borne locusts and a khamsin dust storm. Colin Humphreys and others have refined the idea. Siro Trevisanato linked them to the Thera eruption, though it is usually dated about 1600 BC. Many believers accept natural causes with miraculous timing; others hold that the text describes events beyond nature, coming and going at Moses' word. Critical scholars treat the cycle as a literary composition from several sources. Many also see a polemic against Egypt's gods (Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4).

sections.h: The plagues elsewhere in the Bible
sections.b: Deuteronomy threatens an unfaithful Israel with "the boils of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 28:27). Amos 4:10 recalls plague "after the manner of Egypt." Revelation's trumpets and bowls reuse the plagues: water turned to blood, sores, hail, darkness, locusts, and unclean spirits like frogs. Wisdom of Solomon 11–19 retells the plagues as a long reflection on how God punishes through the very things by which people sin.

common: The plagues show the LORD's power over Egypt and its gods.
uncommon: Greta Hort argued that the first nine plagues form a natural chain of events beginning with an unusually high Nile flood.

sections.b: Exodus mentions Pharaoh's heart about twenty times, with three verbs: chazaq "be strong, stubborn," kaved "be heavy," and qashah "be hard." God foretells the hardening (4:21; 7:3), but the narrator first says that God did it at the sixth plague (9:12). Before then Pharaoh hardens his own heart or it simply "was" hard. In the end God gains "glory," kavod, from the same root as the "heavy" heart (14:4, 17).
sections.refs: Exodus 4:21; Exodus 7:3; Exodus 7:13–14; Exodus 8:15; Exodus 9:12; Exodus 9:34; Exodus 10:1; Exodus 14:4

sections.b: Jewish tradition (Exodus Rabbah, Rashi, Maimonides) reads it as judgment on repeated free choices: after five refusals God closed the door of repentance. Origen: God's same goodness softens some hearts and hardens others, as the sun melts wax and hardens clay. Augustine and Calvin: God's sovereign decree, with Pharaoh still responsible. Sforno, followed by many modern scholars: "made strong" means God gave Pharaoh the nerve to keep choosing freely. Arminians (Arminius, Wesley): God hardens those who first resist. Paul quotes Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17–18.

common: Pharaoh first hardened his own heart, and God then confirmed his choice.
uncommon: The Egyptian picture of a heart weighed after death may stand behind Exodus's "heavy" heart.

sections.b: The early date, about 1446 BC, takes 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years from the exodus to Solomon's fourth year) literally and is defended by Bimson, Wood and Merrill. The late date, about 1260s BC, rests on the store city Rameses (Pi-Ramesses, built by Ramesses II), the settlement of Edom and Moab, and the spread of new villages in Canaan after 1200 BC; Kitchen and Hoffmeier favor it. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) shows that Israel was in Canaan by then. Critical scholars (Finkelstein, Dever) find no archaeological trace of a mass exodus.

Clues debated include Pithom and Rameses (1:11), the 430 years (12:40, longer in the Septuagint and Samaritan text, which include Canaan), the coastal road "by way of the Philistines' land" (13:17), who arrived about 1175 BC, the camels of 9:3, and the Philistia, Edom and Moab of the Song of the Sea (15:14–15). Defenders of an early date explain several of these as later updates of names.
sections.refs: Exodus 1:11; Exodus 9:3; Exodus 12:40; Exodus 13:17; Exodus 15:14–15; Galatians 3:17

common: The exodus is usually dated either about 1446 BC or in the 1200s BC.
uncommon: David Rohl proposed revising Egyptian chronology to place the exodus in an earlier dynasty; most Egyptologists reject this.

sections.b: Hebrew Yam Suf means "Sea of Reeds"; suf is the reed of the Nile where Moses' basket lay (2:3). The Septuagint translated it "Red Sea," and most English versions followed. The locusts are blown into it (10:19), Israel is led toward it (13:18), Pharaoh's officers sink in it (15:4), and Israel leaves it for the wilderness of Shur (15:22). Elsewhere it clearly names the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26).
sections.refs: Exodus 2:3; Exodus 10:19; Exodus 13:18; Exodus 15:4; Exodus 15:22; 1 Kings 9:26

sections.b: Proposals include Lake Sirbonis on the Mediterranean coast; Lake Ballah, Lake Timsah or the Bitter Lakes on the Suez isthmus (Hoffmeier); the Gulf of Suez (the traditional site); and the Gulf of Aqaba (Humphreys). The place names Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon (14:2) are not securely located. Drews and Han (2010) modeled how an all-night east wind could expose a land bridge in the Nile Delta. Bernard Batto argued that the name also carried a mythic sense, "the sea at the end" of the world.

common: The Hebrew name means "Sea of Reeds," while "Red Sea" comes from the Greek translation.
uncommon: Some place the crossing at the Gulf of Aqaba and Mount Sinai in Arabia.

sections.b: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (4:22): Pharaoh's refusal to free God's firstborn is answered by the death of Egypt's firstborn (11:5; 12:29). Because Israel's firstborn were spared, they belong to the LORD: firstborn animals are sacrificed, a firstborn donkey is ransomed with a lamb, and firstborn sons are ransomed (13:2, 11–16). The Levites later take the firstborn's place (Numbers 3:11–13). The Jewish ceremony pidyon ha-ben continues the rite, and Luke tells of Jesus presented as a firstborn (Luke 2:22–23).
sections.refs: Exodus 4:22–23; Exodus 11:5; Exodus 12:29; Exodus 13:2; Exodus 13:11–16; Numbers 3:11–13; Luke 2:22–23

common: Israel's firstborn belong to God because they were spared on the night of Passover.

sections.b: A sister of the baby Moses watches him among the reeds and arranges for his own mother to nurse him (2:4–8); tradition identifies her with Miriam. At the sea she is "Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister," leading the women with frame drums and singing "Sing to the LORD, for he has risen up high" (15:20–21). Many scholars think her short song is older than the longer Song of the Sea, and a Qumran manuscript (4Q365) preserves additional lines of a Song of Miriam.

uncommon: Frank Cross and others suggested the whole Song of the Sea was originally Miriam's song.

sections.b: Aaron enters the story as Moses' older brother and spokesman: "He will become your mouth, and you will become as God to him" (4:16), and "Aaron your brother will be your prophet" (7:1). He meets Moses at the mountain of God, performs the signs before the elders, and with his staff begins the first three plagues. The genealogy of 6:14–27 traces him to Levi and names his wife Elisheba and his sons, the future priests.
sections.refs: Exodus 4:14–16; Exodus 4:27–31; Exodus 6:20–25; Exodus 7:1–2; Exodus 7:9–12; Exodus 8:5–17

sections.b: Hidden in a papyrus ark and named by Pharaoh's daughter, Moses grows up at court, kills an Egyptian, flees to Midian, and marries Zipporah (2). At the burning bush he hears the name of God and raises five objections (3–4). He confronts Pharaoh through ten blows (5–11), leads the first Passover (12), and stretches his hand over the sea (14). By the end Israel "believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant" (14:31). His name is Egyptian (as in Thutmose), explained by a Hebrew pun, "I drew him out."
sections.refs: Exodus 2:1–22; Exodus 3:1–4:17; Exodus 7:1–7; Exodus 14:31; Acts 7:20–36; Hebrews 11:23–29

sections.h: "I will be who I will be" and 6:3
sections.b: At the bush God answers Moses' question with ehyeh asher ehyeh, "I will be who I will be," and gives the name YHWH, "the LORD," as his name forever (3:14–15). Readings range from presence ("I will be there") to being ("I am the one who is," Septuagint) to a refusal to be controlled. In 6:3 God says he appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai, "but my name, the LORD, I did not make known to them," a text explained as a new depth of meaning or as a sign of different sources. Exodus 15 adds the short form Yah and the titles "man of war" and "your healer" (15:3, 26).

sections.h: Egypt as the house of slaves
sections.b: In Exodus Egypt turns from a refuge (Genesis 46–47) into "the house of slaves" (13:3; 20:2). The details are Egyptian: brick quotas, chartummim magicians, Nile worship, chariots, store cities in the eastern Delta. The plagues are framed as judgment "on all the gods of Egypt" (12:12). The Israelites leave with Egyptian silver and gold (12:35–36), which Augustine made a figure for using pagan learning in God's service.
sections.refs: Exodus 1:11–14; Exodus 7:11; Exodus 12:12; Exodus 12:35–36; Exodus 13:3; Genesis 47:27

sections.b: Exodus 1–15 sets the pattern later texts reuse: oppression, a cry heard by God, a deliverer, judgment on the oppressor, a night of escape, a crossing of water, and a song of victory. Isaiah promises a new exodus through the waters (43:16–19; 51:9–11), Hosea and Matthew apply "from Egypt I called my son" to Jesus, and Paul reads the sea as baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). The prophets promise a second exodus greater than the first (Jeremiah 16:14–15; 23:7–8; Micah 7:15; Isaiah 11:15–16; Hosea 2:15), and Luke calls Jesus' coming death his exodos (Luke 9:31).
sections.refs: Luke 9:31; Jeremiah 16:14–15; Micah 7:15; Exodus 2:23–25; Exodus 14:21–31; Exodus 15:1–18; Isaiah 43:16–19; Isaiah 51:9–11; Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2

sections.b: The Passover animal is a seh, a lamb or kid, "a sound and whole animal, a male in its first year" (Exodus 12:5). Its blood marks the houses, and no bone of it is broken (12:46). John's Gospel applies this to Jesus, who dies when the lambs are slaughtered and whose legs are not broken (John 19:36), and Paul calls Christ "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7).
sections.refs: Exodus 12:3–13; Exodus 12:46; John 1:29; John 19:36; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Peter 1:19

sections.h: The mixed crowd and one law
sections.b: A "large mixed crowd" leaves Egypt with Israel (12:38), and some Egyptians who feared the LORD's word had already acted on it (9:20). Passover law separates the outsider who keeps his own identity, who may not eat, from the resident foreigner who circumcises his household, who becomes "like one born in the land." "One law will hold for the one born in the land and for the foreigner" (12:49).

Christian readers have found patterns of Christ throughout these chapters: the infant saved from a murderous king (Exodus 2; Matthew 2), the rejected deliverer (Acts 7:35), the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), the sea as baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), the pillar as Christ the light, and the wood that sweetened Marah as the cross (Justin, Tertullian). Jewish tradition also reads the exodus as a pattern of the final redemption, as in the Targums' "four nights."
sections.refs: Exodus 2:1–10; Exodus 12:42; Exodus 14:22; Exodus 15:25; Matthew 2:13–18; Acts 7:35; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4

sections.b: Exodus 6:3, where God says the patriarchs did not know his name, the LORD, is a cornerstone of source criticism: the Priestly writer held that the name was first revealed to Moses. Exodus 3 and 6 are read as two call stories (E and P), and the plagues and the sea crossing as J and P accounts woven together, which explains, for instance, livestock that die twice (9:6; 9:19–25) and a sea dried by wind and split by Moses' hand (14:21).

The Septuagint and the Qumran scroll 4QExod-b give seventy-five descendants of Jacob in 1:5, as Stephen does (Acts 7:14). The Samaritan Pentateuch and 4QpaleoExod-m expand the plague stories, repeating each command as a report that Moses carried it out. The Septuagint and Samaritan text count the 430 years of 12:40 as time "in Egypt and in the land of Canaan," as Paul's chronology in Galatians 3:17 assumes.

Exodus begins with forced labor: "slave-gang bosses," brick quotas, and lives made "bitter with hard labor" (1:11–14), followed by bricks without straw (5:6–19). God hears the cry and frees the slaves, and his opening words at Sinai name him as the one who brought them "out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves" (20:2). The memory became a moral ground of Israel's laws (Deuteronomy 15:15) and a central text for enslaved Africans in the Americas and for liberation theology.
sections.refs: Exodus 1:11–14; Exodus 2:23–25; Exodus 5:6–19; Exodus 6:5–7; Exodus 13:3; Deuteronomy 15:15

sections.h: The mountain of God in Exodus 3
sections.b: Moses first meets God at "God's mountain, toward Horeb" (3:1), where the bush burns without being eaten up and the ground is holy. The sign God gives is that Israel will serve him "on this mountain" (3:12), and Aaron later meets Moses there (4:27). Some scholars locate it in Midian, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, because Moses was tending Jethro's flock.

sections.h: The angel of the LORD and the destroyer
sections.b: In the bush "the angel of the LORD" appears, yet it is God who speaks (3:2–6). The angel of God moves with the pillar behind Israel at the sea (14:19). On Passover night "the destroyer" is kept out of Israel's houses (12:23), while the Haggadah insists the LORD acted "I and not an angel." Christian writers from Justin Martyr on often identified the angel of the bush with the Son of God before his birth; Jewish interpreters saw a created messenger through whom God spoke.

sections.h: Bridegroom of blood and the Passover rule
sections.b: On the road to Egypt, Zipporah circumcises her son to stop the LORD's attack, calling Moses "a bridegroom of blood" (4:24–26), a scene the Talmud explains as punishment for delay. Circumcision becomes the requirement for any outsider who would eat the Passover (12:44, 48): a bought slave or a resident foreigner who is circumcised may eat it and becomes "like one born in the land." Joshua renews circumcision before Israel's first Passover in Canaan.

The priest of Midian appears first as Reuel, father of seven daughters whom Moses rescues at a well (2:16–21). He welcomes the Egyptian-looking stranger, gives him his daughter Zipporah, and Moses tends his flocks for years. Moses is herding "the sheep and goats of Jethro, his father-in-law" when he comes to the burning bush (3:1), and he asks Jether's (Jethro's) leave before returning to Egypt (4:18). The different names, Reuel, Jethro and Jether, have been explained as a grandfather and grandson (Rashi), as names and titles of one man, or as traces of different sources. Many scholars connect his priesthood with the origins of Israel's worship of the LORD (the Midianite or Kenite hypothesis).

sections.h: Glory over Pharaoh, glory in the cloud
sections.b: Exodus plays on the root kaved, "heavy." Pharaoh makes his heart "heavy" (8:15, 32), and God answers, "I will win glory for myself through Pharaoh" (14:4, 17), using the same root: God's weight, his kavod, is felt through the king who resisted him. The pillar of cloud and fire that leads Israel (13:21–22) and stands between the camps at the sea (14:19–20) is the first form of the glory that will later rest on Sinai and fill the tabernacle (24:16–17; 40:34–38).
sections.refs: Exodus 8:15; Exodus 13:21–22; Exodus 14:4; Exodus 14:17–20; Exodus 16:10; Exodus 40:34–38
